strengths: The paper studies a practically relevant intersection of domain generalization and learning with noisy labels that is underexplored relative to either problem in isolation.
DL4ND is intuitive and simple: it uses low-loss, class-domain prototypes and cross-domain comparisons to reduce reliance on domain-specific similarities when correcting labels.
The empirical study covers two real-world and two synthetically corrupted datasets and includes a broad collection of recent DG and noisy-label baselines, as well as several combined baselines.

The results provide useful evidence that naive combinations of DG and noisy-label methods can interact poorly, and DL4ND often improves both ID and OOD accuracy, especially under substantial synthetic noise.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is unsupported and appears invalid as stated. Theorem 1 is presented without a proof, and Assumption 1—which compares distance to a same-class mean against distance to a same-domain mean—does not imply separation from every alternative-class cross-domain mean. The assumption also largely presupposes the invariant representation that the method seeks to learn.

Critical experimental and implementation details are missing. Appendix B.2, titled “Synthesized Noise,” is empty; the paper does not specify the full corruption procedure, validation protocol, hyperparameters, GMM configuration, label-update timing criterion, handling of missing class-domain proxies, or whether correction is performed once or repeatedly. No complete DL4ND algorithm is provided.

All results are reported as single numbers without variation over random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Several important real-dataset advantages are small—for example, the best CHAMMI-CP average improves by less than one point over the strongest non-DL4ND combination—so robustness of the conclusions cannot be assessed.

Model and hyperparameter selection are unclear, particularly the claimed determination of an “optimal label update step.” Without specifying what validation labels or domains are used, it is impossible to rule out target-domain or clean-label information leakage.

The construction of the real-world evaluation is insufficiently validated. VLCS noise labels come from unspecified manual inspection with no annotation protocol, number of annotators, agreement statistics, or released annotations. Many listed “noisy” examples appear to be multi-object or difficult images rather than demonstrably incorrect labels.

The CHAMMI-CP interpretation is conceptually questionable: treatment identity is an experimental condition, while a weak or visually control-like cellular response does not necessarily make the treatment label incorrect. Relabeling such examples based on phenotype may change the intended prediction target, undermining the claim that this experiment evaluates label-noise correction.

Ablations are inadequate. The paper does not isolate cross-domain comparison from ordinary global class prototypes, within-domain prototypes, low-loss filtering, alternative confidence criteria, or simple nearest-prototype relabeling. It also lacks noise-detection precision/recall and corrected-label accuracy on the main synthetic datasets, making the proposed mechanism difficult to verify.

Reproducibility and fairness remain weak despite the many baselines: training budgets and tuning procedures are not documented consistently, computational costs are not compared, and the promised code is not sufficient to compensate for the missing methodology in the submitted paper. Overall, the idea is promising, but the unsupported theory and incomplete evaluation prevent acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant intersection of domain generalization and learning with noisy labels that is underexplored relative to either problem alone.
The proposed use of cross-domain class proxies is intuitive, simple, and compatible with several established DG algorithms.
The empirical study covers real and synthetic noise, ID and OOD accuracy, and a broad collection of DG/LNL baselines and combinations.
Some gains are substantial, particularly on VLCS and in high-noise synthetic settings.
weaknesses: The central theoretical justification is unsound as written. Assumption 1 compares distance to a class mean against distance to a domain mean, but it does not imply Theorem 1's stronger separation from every alternative class. No proof is given, and the theorem relies on true-label conditional expectations that are unavailable to the algorithm.

The evaluation lacks repeated-run variation, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. Consequently, modest gains—especially the sub-one-point improvement over the strongest comparator on CHAMMI-CP—cannot be distinguished from training variance.

Critical experimental details are missing. Appendix B.2 is empty, while optimizer settings, learning rates, hyperparameter selection, GMM fitting, feature layer, label-update timing, number of updates, and handling of missing class-domain proxies are not specified adequately.

The proposed components are not isolated. There is no controlled ablation of cross-domain versus same-domain prototypes, low-loss filtering, GMM separation, update timing, or alternative prototype constructions, so the claimed mechanism is not established.

The real-world label-noise evaluation is questionable. VLCS test samples are manually removed as noisy without an annotation protocol, number of annotators, agreement analysis, or evidence that this curation was independent of method development. For CHAMMI-CP, weak treatment response is treated as label corruption even though the treatment identity may remain factually correct, making the target task and relabeling semantics unclear.

Synthetic evaluation is narrow: class pairs are manually chosen, only a few noise rates are tested, and there are no symmetric, instance-dependent, domain-dependent, or naturally occurring corruption controls. Domain-level results are also hidden by averages.

The empirical story is mixed. DL4ND sometimes reduces ID accuracy, improvements vary greatly across DG backbones, and several claimed broad conclusions are based on only two real datasets without analysis explaining these failures.

Novelty is limited: the method is essentially early-learning/GMM sample separation followed by nearest cross-domain prototype relabeling. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish this construction from existing prototype-based noisy-label correction or domain-aware sample-selection methods.

Reproducibility and presentation fall below top-tier standards: the manuscript says code will be released only upon acceptance, the supplement provides lengthy pseudocode for baseline combinations but not a precise DL4ND algorithm, and numerous grammatical and typographical errors impede clarity.

strengths: The paper identifies a practically relevant intersection of domain generalization and learning with noisy labels that is insufficiently studied by either literature alone.
DL4ND is intuitive and simple: low-loss class-domain proxies and cross-domain comparisons form a plug-and-play label-refinement mechanism that can be combined with multiple DG algorithms.
The empirical study is broad, covering two naturally noisy datasets, two controlled synthetic-noise datasets, numerous recent DG and noisy-label baselines, and several naive combinations.
Results are promising in several settings. In particular, DL4ND combinations improve the best reported VLCS ID/OOD average and often provide sizable gains under high synthetic noise.
The discussion of how sample selection can distort domain balance is insightful and could motivate further work on jointly handling noise and distribution shift.
weaknesses: The theoretical foundation is unsound as presented. Theorem 1 does not follow from Assumption 1: proximity to an overall class mean relative to an overall domain mean does not imply that the correct cross-domain class proxy is closer than every incorrect-class proxy. No proof or additional conditions are provided, and failure of this inequality does not establish that a sample is inherently indistinguishable or noisy.

The experiments omit the central ablations needed to validate the proposed mechanism. There is no controlled comparison against same-domain proxies, domain-agnostic class centroids, prediction-based relabeling, or low-loss selection without cross-domain comparison. Consequently, the gains cannot be specifically attributed to the claimed cross-domain signal.

All tables report single point estimates without numbers of runs, standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests, despite claims of significant improvement. Several important gains are modest, and DL4ND sometimes hurts performance, such as ERM++ ID accuracy on OfficeHome; the robustness of the conclusions is therefore unclear.

The real-world noise evaluation is insufficiently validated. The manuscript does not provide annotator counts, agreement, labeling instructions, or a released annotation protocol for VLCS. Many examples involve multi-object scenes, making the distinction between an incorrect label, a small target object, and domain difficulty ambiguous. Similarly, biological non-response to a treatment in CHAMMI-CP is not obviously equivalent to an erroneous class label.

Reproducibility is poor. Appendix B.2, which is supposed to describe synthesized noise, is empty; the label-update time is described only as an 'optimal' step; and key details about GMM fitting, proxy construction edge cases, optimization hyperparameters, data splits, model selection, and random seeds are absent.

The evaluation protocol is not sufficiently specified to rule out selection bias. In particular, the construction of cleaned VLCS test sets, separation of ID training and test samples, use of manual annotations during development, and hyperparameter selection under leave-one-domain-out evaluation are unclear.

The reported average of ID and OOD accuracy gives the two objectives equal weight without justification and can obscure substantial tradeoffs. More informative reporting would include worst-domain results, clean-label or oracle references, noise-detection and corrected-label metrics on the main datasets, and Pareto-style ID/OOD comparisons.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant and underexplored intersection of learning with noisy labels and multi-source domain generalization.
DL4ND is simple and intuitive: it combines low-loss class-domain prototypes with cross-domain comparisons to relabel suspected noisy samples.
The empirical study is broad, covering seven datasets, multiple noise types, numerous DG/LNL baselines and combinations, and component ablations.
Controlled experiments show substantial improvements in several high-noise settings, while relabeling-precision results provide some direct evidence for the proposed mechanism.
weaknesses: All results are reported as single numbers without the number of runs, standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests. This is particularly problematic because many headline improvements on real-world datasets are only 1–2 percentage points.

The status of VLCS, PACS, and CHAMMI-CP as genuinely noisy-label benchmarks is insufficiently established. Multi-object images, missing secondary annotations, weak treatment phenotypes, and intrinsically ambiguous examples are treated as label noise without a rigorous annotation protocol or independent ground truth.

Reproducibility details are incomplete despite the reproducibility claim: dataset-specific optimization settings, random seeds, model-selection protocol, warmup choices, GMM configuration, feature extraction details, and complete DL4ND pseudocode are missing. The sensitivity analysis itself indicates that warmup selection can materially affect OOD performance.

The method is technically incremental, largely combining established small-loss/GMM selection and prototype-based label correction; the cross-domain restriction is useful but represents a relatively modest methodological advance.

Some conclusions are stronger than the evidence. DL4ND occasionally reduces ID performance, and the ERM++ ablation on CHAMMI-CP performs slightly better without relabeling on the reported average, contradicting the claim that every component consistently improves performance. The claimed 3–18% ERM improvement also does not transparently match the absolute differences in the corresponding table.

The global loss-based GMM used to select trustworthy samples can itself favor easy domains—the failure mode attributed to prior LNL methods. Grouping selected samples afterward does not clearly eliminate this bias, and a per-domain selection ablation is absent.

strengths: The paper identifies a practically relevant intersection of noisy-label learning and domain generalization, including the plausible failure mode that conventional noisy-label selection can disproportionately discard difficult domains.
DL4ND is simple and modular: it combines low-loss sample selection, class-domain prototypes, and cross-domain relabeling, and can be integrated with several domain-generalization methods.

The empirical scope is substantial, covering seven datasets, real and synthetic noise, multiple noise levels, numerous DG/LNL baselines and combinations, component ablations, relabeling precision, and warmup sensitivity.
Several controlled-noise experiments show sizable improvements in both in-domain and out-of-domain accuracy, so the central cross-domain-comparison idea has promising empirical evidence.
weaknesses: The paper reports no results across random seeds, standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Many important real-data improvements are only approximately 0.3–2 percentage points, making the conclusions difficult to distinguish from training and model-selection variance.

The validity of the claimed real-world noise is questionable. In VLCS and PACS, images are counted as noisy when another target category co-occurs, even when the assigned category is visibly present. This is multi-label ambiguity rather than conventional label corruption, and the manual annotation protocol, annotator agreement, and treatment of ambiguous cases are not documented. The characterization of CHAMMI-CP noise is also insufficiently detailed.

The evaluation and model-selection protocol is underspecified: it is unclear how validation sets are constructed, whether target-domain information is completely excluded when choosing warmup length and other hyperparameters, how competing methods are tuned, and whether synthetic-noise realizations are averaged. These omissions materially affect a DG evaluation.

The synthetic asymmetric corruption schemes are manually chosen without adequate justification. The DomainNet mapping is given only as hundreds of numeric indices, is heavily concentrated on a few destination classes, and is not interpretable as a set of semantically plausible confusions. This limits confidence that the reported large gains generalize beyond favorable corruption constructions.

The technical presentation is incomplete. Equation 2 applies a distance to sets without a precise definition and invokes true class membership despite true labels being unknown. There is no theoretical or systematic empirical justification for selecting the single nearest proxy from another domain, nor clear handling of missing or unreliable class-domain proxies, non-bimodal loss distributions, or domains whose low-loss samples remain noisy.

The novelty is moderate: the method largely combines established small-loss/GMM selection and prototype-based pseudo-labeling, with cross-domain restriction as the main new ingredient. Comparisons to simpler matched alternatives such as domain-balanced selection, averaged cross-domain prototypes, cross-domain consistency, or other prototype relabeling variants are limited.

The ablations do not consistently support the stated claim that every component improves performance. For example, on CHAMMI-CP with ERM++, removing relabeling slightly improves average accuracy, while removing cross-domain comparison substantially improves OOD accuracy. Without uncertainty estimates, these mixed outcomes are unresolved.

Reproducibility remains inadequate despite the paper's claim of released code: the manuscript lacks a complete DL4ND algorithm and exact hyperparameters, relabeling schedule, feature layer and normalization choices, GMM details, training budgets for all datasets, and compute or runtime overhead. The claim of no additional overhead is not measured.

strengths: The paper identifies a practically important and underexplored setting—simultaneous label noise and domain shift—and clearly explains why standard LNL and DG methods can fail when applied independently or naively combined.

DL4ND is simple, intuitive, and readily composable with multiple DG methods. Using low-loss class–domain prototypes and cross-domain comparisons is well motivated by the observation that domain-specific spurious features can mislead within-domain relabeling.
The empirical evaluation is broad, covering seven datasets, real and synthetic noise, multiple noise types, both ID and OOD accuracy, and numerous LNL, DG, and combined baselines.

The ablations directly test the main design choices: relabeling versus removal, cross-domain versus within-domain comparison, and low-loss versus all-sample prototypes. Relabeling-precision results and the analysis of domain imbalance in UNICON further support the proposed mechanism.

Results are consistently favorable overall, including substantial improvements under severe synthetic noise and smaller but meaningful gains on real-world datasets. The appendices provide noise mappings, sensitivity experiments, integration algorithms, and discussion of related domain-adaptation work.
The presentation is generally clear, with useful diagrams and an appropriate discussion of limitations and ethical considerations.
weaknesses: All principal tables report point estimates without standard deviations, confidence intervals, or the number of random seeds. Several claimed gains are below one percentage point, so their statistical reliability cannot be assessed.

Model-selection and hyperparameter protocols are insufficiently specified. In particular, it is unclear how warmup length, relabeling frequency, GMM settings, and baseline-specific hyperparameters are selected without access to clean labels or the held-out target domain. The sensitivity results also show that the warmup choice can materially affect performance.

The treatment of real-world noise needs stronger validation. VLCS noise appears to be established partly through manual inspection of missing multi-label annotations, while PACS noise is only briefly characterized and CHAMMI-CP ambiguity is not clearly separated from actual annotation errors. It is also unclear whether ID and OOD test annotations were independently cleaned; evaluation against noisy test labels could confound the conclusions.

Reproducibility details for DL4ND itself are incomplete despite the stated code release: the paper does not fully specify whether the GMM is global or group-conditioned, how empty or very small class–domain proxy groups are handled, exactly when labels are updated, and the complete per-dataset training and hyperparameter configurations. The manuscript’s code link is also blank in the reviewed version.

The method assumes known, discrete, and reliable domain labels, with every relevant class sufficiently represented across domains. The paper does not investigate missing classes, imbalanced domains, incorrect domain metadata, continuous domain shifts, or settings where domains share the same spurious correlations.

The conceptual novelty is moderate: the method combines established small-loss selection, prototype-based correction, and domain-aware comparison. Its strongest contribution is the formulation and empirical study of the joint setting rather than a major technical advance.

Some comparisons could be more controlled. The paper explores many DG–LNL combinations but does not provide compute-matched comparisons, exhaustive tuning details, or results against a domain-aware adaptation of each strongest LNL baseline. The cross-domain precision analysis is also limited to two synthetic-noise datasets.
